title: AI Foundry Lab
text:
Course Numbers
The BYU AI Foundry is a sponsored-project studio inside the BYU Marriott School of Business. Client organizations bring a real, open-ended business problem. A small team of high-performing students, guided by faculty, spends an academic year designing, prototyping, and testing an AI-enabled solution to it.
The Foundry is not an internship placement and not a research project. It is delivery work. Every engagement ends with something the client can use: a working prototype, a decision framework with the rules written down, a model whose outputs can be explained, and a recommendation the client’s leadership can act on.
Students typically complete MSB 341 - Product Management before joining a Foundry team, so they arrive with product and applied AI skills already built.
This course is cross-listed under two course numbers. It is all the same class: everyone meets together Fridays 8:00 to 11:50 AM in 2140 TNRB, works on the same client teams, uses this site, and is graded on the same rubric. Register under whichever number fits your program.
Mixed MBA and undergraduate teams are intentional. Client engagements benefit from the range, and it mirrors how real delivery teams are staffed.

section: What Makes This Different from an Engineering Capstone
text:
What Makes This Different from an Engineering Capstone
The BYU engineering capstones build physical and embedded systems: CAD, prototypes, PCBs, firmware, security assessments. The AI Foundry builds business decision systems: strategy frameworks, prioritization and scoring models, forecasting and predictive analytics, financial models, and the software that makes those things usable by a decision maker.
If the question is “how do we build this thing,” that is engineering. If the question is “which things should we build, in what order, and how do we know,” that is the Foundry.

title: Syllabus
text:
Confidentiality and Client Data
Foundry clients share confidential business information: financials, pipelines, customer data, and strategy. This is a condition of the work, and it carries obligations.

You will sign the client’s NDA, or the Foundry’s standard mutual NDA, before receiving data.
Client data stays in the approved project repository and approved tools. It does not go into personal accounts, personal cloud storage, or unapproved AI services.
Nothing about the project goes on LinkedIn, in a portfolio, or in a job interview without written client permission. Ask the program director first, every time.
Deliverables and intellectual property belong to the client, not to you and not to BYU.
When the project ends, you delete local copies of client data.

A confidentiality breach is an Honor Code matter and will also end the engagement. Treat this as the professional obligation it is.

title: Syllabus
text:
AI Use Policy
You are expected to use AI tools aggressively. That is the point of the Foundry. The obligations that come with it:

You own the output. “The model produced it” is not a defense for a wrong number, a fabricated citation, or an analysis you cannot explain.
Every deliverable must be explainable. If you cannot walk the client through why the model recommends what it recommends, it is not done.
Client data goes only into approved tools. See the confidentiality section above.
Disclose method, not apology. Milestone documentation should say what tools and models you used and how you validated the output.

Instructor Bio
Scott Murff is an Associate Teaching Professor of Strategy at the BYU Marriott School of Business, where he also serves as program director and teaches courses on business strategy, decision-making, and artificial intelligence. He brings over 15 years of experience at the intersection of business and technology, having worked as a consultant, product manager, and data scientist.
Prior to joining BYU, Scott spent nearly seven years at McKinsey & Company in roles ranging from analytics specialist consultant to principal product manager, where he led product development and performance management initiatives for Fortune 500 clients. His earlier career includes building forecasting models as a VP at Zions Bancorporation and conducting regulatory research at the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.
Scott holds a Master’s degree in Management Science & Engineering from Stanford University and a B.A. in Economics with a minor in Math, from BYU. He is passionate about helping students apply AI, analytics, and strategy to meaningful real-world problems with both rigor and purpose.

Mission and Aims
The mission of Brigham Young University — founded, supported, and guided by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints: is to assist individuals in their quest for perfection and eternal life. That assistance should provide a period of intensive learning in a stimulating setting where a commitment to excellence is expected and the full realization of human potential is pursued.
BYU seeks to develop students of faith, intellect, and character who have the skills and the desire to continue learning and to serve others throughout their lives.
A BYU education should be (1) spiritually strengthening, (2) intellectually enlarging, and (3) character building, leading to (4) lifelong learning and service.
Building on the foundational Mission and Aims, the Marriott School of Business aspires to transform the world through Christlike leadership by developing leaders of faith, intellect, and character guided by the following 4 values:

Faith in Christ - We value deep and abiding faith in Jesus Christ. Our faith gives us the capacity to envision a better future, the confidence to make that future happen, and the courage to act in the face of challenges.
Integrity in Action - We value integrity and hold ourselves to the highest moral and ethical standards. Acting with integrity builds trust, strengthens character, and focuses our ambitions on things of eternal consequence.
Respect for All - We value respect for all individuals as children of God and recognize the inherent worth, divine potential, and agency of each person. A climate of respect and belonging enhances our learning, facilitates collaboration, and encourages personal growth.
Excellence - We value excellence in learning, teaching, research, management, and leadership. An expectation of excellence magnifies our influence and motivates us to continually improve.

We evaluate our decisions and actions by the impact they will have on the academic experience, professional preparation, character development, emotional well-being, and spiritual growth of our students.

text:
Example Email
Subject: AI Foundry Weekly Update - [Client] - Week of Oct 5

Hi [Name],

Accomplished this week:
- Scored 42 of the 60 candidate products against the draft criteria. 11 clear
  the NPV multiple threshold of 3.0x under base-case assumptions.
- Reconciled the revenue baseline to your FY26 actuals. We were off by 2.3%
  on specialty; the gap was a channel mapping issue, now corrected.
- Drafted the sensitivity structure for price erosion and launch timing.

Priorities for next week:

- Run the first full sensitivity pass and identify which rankings are fragile (Ana)

- If the gross-to-net data is not available by Oct 12, the M1 framework will

[Client lead name], on behalf of the [Client] Foundry team

title: Weekly Updates
text:
What Makes an Update Good

Lead with the number or the finding. “11 of 42 products clear the threshold” beats “continued portfolio scoring.”
Name owners. Unowned priorities do not get done.
Ask for what you need explicitly. Clients cannot read minds, and a blocker you did not raise is your fault, not theirs.
Flag risk early and unemotionally. A risk raised in week 4 is a conversation. The same risk surfaced in week 12 is a failure.
Never pad. A short honest week is fine. A long week of activity with no outcomes is not.

title: Build Standards
text:
The Four Dimensions
Milestones are graded against these standards. They are also what separates work a client pays for from work a client tolerates.
Every deliverable is scored on correctness, usefulness, explainability, and craft.

title: Build Standards
text:
Correctness

Every number in a client-facing document traces to a source you can point to
Totals reconcile. If your revenue baseline is 2% off the client’s actuals, you find out why before you present it, not after they do
Assumptions are written down as assumptions, with the value used and the reason for it
If you do not know something, the deliverable says so. Fabricated precision is worse than an honest range



Usefulness

The deliverable answers the question the client actually asked
A decision maker can act on it without a translation layer
Recommendations name what to do, not merely what is interesting
Scope creep is not usefulness. If the client’s question changed, renegotiate it in writing



Explainability
This is the standard the Foundry is built around, and it is where AI-assisted work most often fails.

For any model output, you can state which inputs drove it and by how much
Rankings come with sensitivity: what would have to change for the order to change
A model no one on the team can explain is not shippable, regardless of how good the output looks
“The model said so” is never an answer to a client question



Craft

The repository is clean, has a README, and someone outside the team could run it
Documents are proofread. Charts are labeled. Slides have a point per slide
File naming is consistent and dated
No client data in personal accounts, personal repos, or unapproved tools

title: Build Standards
text:
Repository Standards
Every engagement has one private repository in the ai-foundry-byu GitHub organization, named client-<slug>.
client-<slug>/
  README.md          What this is, how to run it, who to ask
  data/              Never committed. Documented in README, stored per client agreement
  analysis/          Notebooks and scripts, in order, that reproduce every number
  model/             The model itself, with its assumptions in one place
  deliverables/      What the client actually receives, versioned by milestone
  docs/              Meeting notes, decision log, scope changes
Two rules that are not negotiable:

No secrets or client data in the repository. Ever. Credentials live in the client’s own systems or an approved secret store.
Every number in a deliverable is reproducible from something in analysis/. If you cannot rerun it, you cannot defend it.

title: Build Standards
text:
The Decision Log
Keep docs/decisions.md current. One entry per material decision:
2026-10-09: Price erosion assumption
Decision: Use 12% annual erosion for specialty, 18% for hospital, rather than a
flat 15% across the portfolio.
Why: Client's 2023-2025 actuals show materially different curves by channel.
Who: Confirmed with Brian Guy on the Oct 8 call.
Reversible: Yes. Sensitivity range 8-22% is built into the model.
This is the single highest-leverage habit in the course. It is what lets you answer “why did you assume that” six months later, and it is what makes handoff possible.

title: Build Standards
text:
QC Gate
Nothing goes to the client without the QC lead’s sign-off. The QC lead checks:

Every number traces to a source
Totals reconcile against the client’s own figures where those exist
Assumptions are stated, with values and reasons
Model outputs are explainable in plain language
Sensitivity is shown for anything presented as a ranking or a recommendation
No client data or secrets in the repository
Document is proofread, charts are labeled, filenames are clean

A milestone that fails QC after it reaches the client costs the whole team craft points. Catch it internally.

title: Build Standards
text:
Working with AI
Use AI tools hard. They are why a team of five can deliver what used to take fifteen.

Generate freely, verify always. Treat every model output as a draft from a fast, capable, occasionally confident-and-wrong analyst.
Check citations and figures by hand. Fabricated sources have ended real consulting engagements.
Keep client data out of unapproved tools. See the confidentiality terms in the Syllabus.
Document your method. Milestone documentation should state which tools you used, for what, and how you validated the output. This is not a confession, it is methodology.

What Sponsorship Covers
The $22,000 fee covers faculty oversight and direction, student team time across two semesters, software and API costs, data and tooling access, program administration, and the final delivery showcase.

title: Program Overview
text:
What We Deliver
The Foundry builds business decision systems. Typical deliverables:

Strategy assessment and validation
Decision frameworks with explicit criteria and thresholds
Scoring and prioritization models
Forecasting and predictive analytics
Financial models, including NPV, sensitivity, and scenario analysis
Optimization under real capital, capacity, and resource constraints
Executive decision dashboards and prototype applications
Executive-ready synthesis and recommendations

Every deliverable carries an explainability requirement: your team can walk you through which assumptions drive each recommendation and what would have to change for the answer to change.

title: Program Overview
text:
What We Do Not Do
Being clear about this saves everyone time.

Production software. We deliver working prototypes and models, not systems hardened for your production environment.
Staff augmentation. This is not a way to get cheap analyst hours on your existing backlog.
Work that is already scoped and specified. If you know exactly what you want built, hire a contractor. The Foundry is for open-ended problems where the answer is not known yet.
Regulated or safety-critical deliverables. Nothing we produce should be relied on as a clinical, legal, financial, or regulatory determination without your own review.

title: Program Overview
section: How This Differs from the Engineering Capstone
text:
How This Differs from the Engineering Capstone
BYU’s engineering capstone programs build physical and embedded systems: CAD, prototypes, PCBs, firmware, security assessments. The AI Foundry builds business decision systems.
If your question is “how do we build this thing,” that is an engineering capstone. If your question is “which things should we build, in what order, and how would we know,” that is the Foundry.

title: Working with the Team
text:
Your Responsibilities as a Sponsor
The engagements that go well share one trait: the sponsor treats the team like a delivery team, not like a class project. This guide covers how to do that in about an hour a week.

title: Working with the Team
text:
Name one point of contact with authority to answer scope questions
Hold a standing weekly call, 30 to 45 minutes, same time every week
Provide data access early. Data delays are the single most common cause of a missed milestone
Answer decision requests within a week. The weekly update will list them explicitly
Attend the four milestone reviews
Complete the mid-term and end-of-term evaluations

title: Working with the Team
text:
Before the Project Starts

Write down the decision you are actually trying to make. Not the analysis you want, the decision it feeds
Identify what data exists, where it lives, and who controls access
Decide what is confidential and what NDA the team should sign
Name your point of contact and a backup
Prepare a 30 minute background briefing for the kick-off

title: Working with the Team
text:
The First Month Is Scoping
Expect the team to push back on the problem statement. That is the design of the program, not a sign of confusion. A team that accepts a vague brief in September delivers a vague answer in April.
By M1 in mid-October you will have a written problem statement, agreed decision criteria, and a definition of success. You sign off on it. Everything after that is measured against it.






Tip



The most valuable hour you will spend on this project is the scoping conversation in week 3. Bring your real constraints: budget, capacity, political reality, what has already been tried. Teams that know the constraints solve the actual problem.

title: Working with the Team
text:
Weekly Cadence







When
What




Standing call
30 to 45 minutes. Team presents progress, you answer open decisions


Saturday
Client lead sends the weekly written update


As needed
Team raises blockers within 48 hours of hitting them, not at the next call



The weekly update has a fixed format: what was accomplished, next week’s priorities with owners, decisions or input needed from you, and any risks. The third section is the one to read first.

title: Working with the Team
text:
Effective Sponsorship

Be specific. “This isn’t quite right” costs a week. “The margin assumption ignores our gross-to-net” costs an hour
Be timely. Feedback at the milestone review is too late to change the milestone
Balance. These are students doing professional work. Tell them what is working, then what is not
Push on rigor, not on volume. Ask “what would have to be true for this to be wrong.” That question makes the work better than any request for more slides

title: Working with the Team
text:
Scope Changes
Businesses change and scopes change with them. The rule is simply that changes are written down.

Raise the change on the weekly call
The team documents it in the decision log and confirms it in the weekly update
If it materially changes the milestone plan, the faculty director is looped in

What does not work is quiet expansion: a new question added each week without anything coming off the plan. The team is instructed to surface that pattern to the faculty director.

title: Working with the Team
text:
If Something Is Not Working
Tell us early. Contact Scott Murff directly at scott.murff@byu.edu. Most problems are fixable in week 5 and unfixable in week 20. Early intervention is not an escalation, it is normal program operation.

title: Evaluation
text:
Feedback Survey
Sponsors complete a brief feedback survey twice: at mid-year for developmental purposes, and at the end of the year as an input into student grades.
The survey asks you to evaluate the team on five dimensions, each on a 1 to 7 scale:
You will also be able to comment on each dimension. Comments are shared with the students.
You evaluate the team, not individual students. Individual differentiation comes from confidential peer evaluation within the team, which is our job to administer, not yours.

title: Evaluation
text:
Timeliness: Meeting deadlines and showing up prepared
Communication: Clarity and effectiveness in writing and in meetings
High Agency: Taking initiative, solving problems proactively, working independently
Technical Competency: Skill in analysis, modeling, and building

title: Evaluation
text:
Mid-Year Feedback
The mid-year survey gives the team a chance to understand where they stand with half the year left. It has no impact on grades. Its purpose is to let them course-correct while there is still time.
After completing it, have a live conversation with the team. Schedule it within a week. This conversation is one of the most valuable parts of the program for students.

Mid-Year Conversation Guide






Tip



Make it two-way. Ask the team for their feedback on the engagement and on what you could do differently as a sponsor. They will have opinions and will be reluctant to volunteer them.



Strengths: What is going well? What should they keep doing?
Growth areas: Where do they need to be sharper by April?
Support: What can you do to help? Data access, introductions, faster decisions?
Scope check: Is the M1 problem statement still the right problem?
Ask for feedback: How can you be a better sponsor?

title: Evaluation
text:
End-of-Year Feedback
The end-of-year survey is the final evaluation and a graded input. It is shared with students, so please discuss it verbally as part of a wrap-up conversation.

Wrap-Up Conversation Guide

Highlights: What did they deliver that you will actually use?
Growth areas: What skills should they develop before their first job?
Career advice: What would help them succeed in this kind of work?
What happens next: Will you act on the recommendation? Is there a follow-on engagement, an internship, or a hire here?
Ask for their feedback: What could the Foundry do better?

title: Evaluation
text:
Student Feedback on the Engagement
At the end of the year we also ask students to evaluate the engagement: quality of mentorship, whether the work mattered, clarity of expectations, and access to data and decisions. We share the results with you. It is the most direct read you will get on how to sponsor better next time.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text: Cost and Terms

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
What does it cost?
$22,000 per project for the full academic year. This matches the BYU engineering capstone sponsorship fee.


What does the fee cover?
Faculty oversight and direction, student team time across two semesters, software and API costs, data and tooling access, program administration, and the final delivery showcase.


When is payment due?
Payment terms and vendor setup are handled through BYU. Contact the program director and we will connect you with the right administrative contact early, so vendor onboarding does not delay the project start.


Is there a formal agreement?
Yes. Sponsorship is confirmed in writing before the project starts, covering scope, fee, IP, and confidentiality.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
Intellectual Property and Confidentiality

Who owns the work?
You do. Sponsors retain all deliverables and intellectual property, including code, models, documents, and analysis.


Will students sign an NDA?
Yes. Every student on the team signs your NDA, or the Foundry’s standard mutual NDA if you prefer. This happens before any data is shared.


How is our data handled?
Client data stays in the approved project repository and approved tools. It does not go into students’ personal accounts, personal cloud storage, or unapproved AI services. Students delete local copies at the end of the engagement. Data handling terms can be tightened to match your requirements.


Can students talk about the project publicly?
Not without your written permission. That includes LinkedIn, portfolios, and job interviews. The default is that the engagement is confidential. Many sponsors do grant permission for a general description, which helps students and costs you nothing, but it is your call.


Do you use AI tools on our data?
Yes, that is the point of the program, and it is governed. Students use approved tools only, under your data handling terms. If you have a specific list of permitted or prohibited AI services, tell us at kick-off and we will scope the toolchain to it.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
Scope and Fit

What makes a strong project?
An open-ended business question where the answer is not known in advance, where the decision recurs so a repeatable framework is worth more than a one-off analysis, and where enough data exists for the team to work with. See the RFP for detail.


What makes a weak project?
A task that is already specified and just needs hands, work that requires proprietary systems access we cannot get, anything safety- or compliance-critical, or a question whose answer you already know and want validated.


Can the scope change mid-year?
Yes, in writing. Changes get documented in the decision log and confirmed in the weekly update. What we manage against is quiet expansion, where questions are added without anything coming off the plan.


What if the project isn’t going well?
Contact the program director immediately. Most engagement problems are fixable in week 5. Early intervention is normal program operation, not an escalation.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
Working Arrangements

How much of my time does this take?
About an hour a week: a 30 to 45 minute standing call, plus reading the weekly update and answering the decisions it asks for. Plus four milestone reviews across the year.


Do we need to be local to Utah?
No. Engagements run remote by default. On-site visits are welcome but not required.


Do we provide equipment or accounts?
Students use their own machines. You may need to provision accounts for data or systems access, which we will scope at kick-off.


Can we hire the students?
Yes, and many sponsors do. Recruiting access is one of the real benefits of sponsorship. Please route offers through the program director during the engagement so it does not disrupt the team.


Can we extend or run a second project?
Yes. Follow-on engagements and paid summer extensions are both common. Extensions are optional and not part of the base program.

Program Overview
The AI Foundry is a year-long applied program running September 2, 2026 through April 14, 2027. It sits inside the Marriott School’s Strategic Management program and is cross-listed for MBA and senior undergraduate students (MBA 693R and STRAT 490R).
Where BYU’s engineering capstones build physical and embedded systems, the AI Foundry builds business decision systems: strategy frameworks, prioritization and scoring models, forecasting and predictive analytics, financial models, and the software that puts those in front of a decision maker.

title: Request for Proposals
text:
Ideal Project Types
Strong fits include:

Portfolio and resource allocation: which products, markets, or investments deserve scarce capital and management attention
AI-enabled decision support: turning a recurring judgment call into a repeatable, evidence-based framework
Forecasting and predictive analytics: demand, revenue, price, churn, risk
Market entry and commercialization: where to play and how to win in a new category
Build, buy, or partner evaluation: structured evaluation of strategic options
Business model evaluation: pricing, channel, and unit economics analysis
Product strategy and prototyping: defining and building toward a new product direction
Operational analytics: decision systems for recurring operating choices

The strongest projects share three traits: the answer is genuinely not known in advance, the decision recurs so a framework is worth more than a one-off analysis, and enough data exists for the team to work with.
Poor fits: work that is already fully specified and just needs hands, staff augmentation on an existing backlog, production software engineering, projects requiring systems access that cannot be provisioned, and safety-, clinical-, or compliance-critical determinations.
